name: Facial yoga / face exercises

card.summary: Muscle exercises for the face promoted as a natural facelift; no study of appearance outcomes exists.
card.aka: face yoga, facial exercises, face workouts
card.note: No study has measured appearance change; forum members themselves rank exercises below surgery or appliances.

quick.overview:
Facial yoga and face exercises are routines of deliberate facial-muscle movements, often shown on video, that proponents say tone the cheeks, chin and jaw and soften the signs of ageing. Looksmaxxing communities discuss them as a low-cost option for the cheekbones, chin and jawline.
No clinical study of their effect on appearance is available. Research that exists on facial exercises concerns older adults' mental health, not facial appearance.
quick.mechanism: The idea is that strengthening facial muscles lifts and fills the overlying skin, much as exercise builds other muscles. Forum users who discuss the topic add that fat loss and chewing are what change facial shape, and some describe the exercises as a fallback for people who cannot afford surgery.
quick.risks: No harms are documented. A forum guide describes the exercises as inferior to surgery, appliances or fillers and as better than nothing for young or low-budget users.

lead: Facial yoga, also called face exercises or face workouts, is a set of voluntary facial-muscle movements promoted to firm, lift or reshape the face, and is often presented as a natural alternative to cosmetic procedures. People practise it, usually from video routines, with the aim of fuller-looking cheeks, a more defined jawline or chin, and smoother expression lines. [1][2] In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed for the cheekbones, nose, chin and jawline. [1]

The reasoning given by proponents is that the face contains many small skeletal muscles that, like muscles elsewhere, can be trained, and that larger, firmer muscles would lift and fill the overlying skin. The practice sits alongside myofunctional therapy, manual facial massage and chewing-based jaw training such as masseter development. [7][8][14]

Published research on appearance outcomes is small but exists. A 2018 pilot study in JAMA Dermatology from Northwestern University had 16 women aged 40 to 65 complete a 20-week exercise programme and reported that blinded raters scored upper and lower cheek fullness as improved and estimated participants as younger, from about 50.8 to 48.1 years, while the authors noted the small sample, dropouts and lack of a control group. [6][11] A 2024 systematic review of myofunctional speech therapy for facial rejuvenation included 21 studies [7], and a 2025 systematic review of conservative mechanical techniques included 12 studies with 321 women aged 30 to 70, covering facial exercises, myofunctional therapy and manual massage; its authors reported improvements limited to specific areas such as the cheeks, jawline and eye region, no adverse events, and called for larger randomized trials. [8] Facial exercise programmes in older adults have also been studied for mental health and cognition. [3][4]

paras: Routines combine exaggerated expressions, tongue and jaw movements, self-massage and resistance techniques, and are usually taught by video or in classes. One looksmax.org guide breaks them into targets for the cheekbones, nose, chin and jawline, including a weighted variation of mewing. [1] Programmes are generally performed daily or several times a week, and the myofunctional therapy literature likewise describes mostly daily practice. [7]

The practice is sometimes grouped with laughter yoga, a separate method developed by Madan Kataria and his wife Madhuri in Mumbai, India, beginning in 1995 and associated with World Laughter Day, which uses forced laughter for mood and wellbeing; face exercises for appearance are a different use of facial movement, aimed at the look of the skin and muscle. [5][12]

Proponents propose that exercising the muscles of the cheeks, jaw and forehead increases muscle bulk and tone, supporting skin that has lost volume with age. The Northwestern authors suggested muscle hypertrophy as a possible explanation for the mid-face and lower-face fullness they observed. [11] The study enrolled people with photodamage and mild to moderate facial atrophy, so the targeted problem was volume loss. [11]

The 2025 systematic review reported improvements limited to specific areas such as the cheeks, jawline and periorbital region, with no adverse events. [8] The 2024 myofunctional review reported gains in wrinkles and frown lines, symmetry and skin elasticity, and better orofacial function, assessed in about 48 percent of studies with objective tools such as cutometers, electromyography and muscle ultrasound. [7] Both reviews' authors note small samples and heterogeneous methods, and the 2025 review concludes that larger randomized trials are needed to establish efficacy. [7][8]
The studies most relevant to appearance are the JAMA Dermatology pilot study and the systematic reviews of facial exercise, myofunctional therapy and massage.

The pilot trial, registered as NCT01689012 and run at Northwestern University, screened 33 eligible adults aged 40 to 65 with photodamage and facial atrophy and enrolled 27; 16 women (mean age 53.7) completed and were analysed. The 20-week protocol had two live 90-minute training sessions with a certified instructor, 30 minutes of daily home exercise from a set of 32 exercises for weeks 1 to 8, then practice every other day for weeks 9 to 20. [11]

Two blinded physicians scored photographs with the Merz-Carruthers photoscales, on which 0 is best and 4 worst. Upper cheek fullness changed from 1.8 to 1.1 and lower cheek fullness from 1.6 to 0.9 (both P = .003), while most other photoscale measures did not change significantly. Raters' age estimates fell from 50.8 to 48.1 years (P = .002), and participants reported higher satisfaction. The authors listed the small all-female sample, 11 dropouts, absence of a control group and self-selection as limitations and called for more research. [11][6]

The 2024 review searched four databases and included 21 studies of myofunctional therapy, reporting fewer wrinkles and frown lines, better symmetry and elasticity, and greater satisfaction, with widely varying assessment tools. [7] The 2025 review, registered on PROSPERO, included 12 studies (six of facial exercise, four of myofunctional therapy and two of manual massage) with 321 women and no male participants. [8]

A Japanese study of 75 community-dwelling adults aged 65 to 87 assessed facial exercises for mental health, and a trial in elderly people with mild cognitive impairment compared walking with hand and face exercises for executive function; neither measured appearance. [3][4] A narrative review of physical activity and skin health describes general exercise as supporting blood flow and sleep, which is distinct from targeted facial exercise. [9] A 2007 Time magazine article on facial yoga is indexed in PubMed. [10]

Mewing, popularised by British orthodontist John Mew and his son Mike under the name orthotropics, involves resting the tongue against the roof of the mouth and is promoted for jaw and face shape. Wikipedia reports that the American Association of Orthodontists has said there is no evidence it improves the jaw, that interest rose from January 2019 with viral spread on social media, and that Mike Mew was struck from the UK dental register in 2024. [13]

The masseter, one of the strongest chewing muscles, is described by Wikipedia as able to enlarge in people who habitually clench or grind their teeth or chew gum constantly, and its enlargement can change facial appearance and symmetry. This is the basis for the forum view that chewing builds the jaw, though chewing is not an exercise programme tested for appearance. [14][1]

The 2025 review reported no adverse events in the included studies. [8] Practitioners and clinicians sometimes raise the question of whether repeated exaggerated expressions could deepen expression lines, a concern that the studies cited here did not measure. Enlargement of the masseter from habitual clenching can produce asymmetry and has been linked to temporomandibular joint problems. [14]

One widely read looksmax.org guide describes face exercises as "copefuel", ranking surgery above appliances, fillers and exercises for results, but says that for young or low-budget people the exercises are better than nothing; its author says a chin routine from a video produced results quickly and recommends them for mildly recessed chins, and also advises cutting body fat and keeping good neck and tongue posture first. [1] A reply in the same thread said the only things that work are losing fat or gaining jaw muscle from chewing. [1] Another thread asks whether a set of exercises is "legit" and draws jokes rather than detailed discussion. [2]

timeline.event: Madan Kataria and Madhuri Kataria begin laughter yoga in Mumbai, a separate facial-movement practice often mentioned alongside face yoga. [12]
World Laughter Day is associated with Kataria's movement, which draws on the facial feedback hypothesis. [5]
Time magazine publishes an article titled Facial yoga. [10]
JAMA Dermatology pilot study (Alam et al.) reports cheek fullness and apparent-age changes after 20 weeks of facial exercise. [6][11]
Interest in mewing begins to rise from January, bringing jaw-focused facial training to social media. [13]
Systematic review of myofunctional speech therapy for facial rejuvenation, 21 studies. [7]
Systematic review of conservative mechanical facial rejuvenation techniques, 12 studies and 321 women. [8]

lore.intro: Face exercises sit near the bottom of the community's usual ranking of methods, behind surgery, appliances and fillers, and are mostly recommended to people with limited options, often alongside fat loss and chewing. [1]

claims.claim: Chin and jaw exercises can produce visible change
claims.believers: A guide's author says a chin exercise from a video produced results quickly for him, advising it for mildly recessed chins. [1]
claims.experts: The 2025 systematic review reported improvements in the jawline and cheek areas in small studies of women aged 30 to 70, and its authors call for larger trials. [8]

claims.claim: Face exercises build the cheeks and lift the face like a natural facelift
claims.believers: Proponents describe training the cheek muscles to add fullness; the guide shares video examples of cheekbone-muscle flexing. [1]
claims.experts: The 2018 Northwestern pilot study reported improved upper and lower cheek fullness in 16 women after 20 weeks, without a control group. [11]

claims.claim: Face exercises are a lesser substitute for surgery or appliances
claims.believers: The same guide says results from surgery, appliances and fillers always exceed exercises. [1]
claims.experts: No comparative studies of exercises against procedures exist. [7][8]

claims.claim: Fat loss and chewing do more than face exercises
claims.believers: A reply says the only effective approaches are losing fat or building jaw muscle by chewing. [1]
claims.experts: Masseter enlargement from habitual clenching or gum chewing is described in the medical literature, though not as an exercise programme tested for appearance. [14]

claims.claim: Weighted mewing or tongue posture shapes the jawline
claims.believers: The guide mentions a weighted mewing variation among its jawline targets, and mewing is widely popular in looksmaxxing spaces. [1][13]
claims.experts: The American Association of Orthodontists has said there is no evidence that mewing improves the jaw, as reported on Wikipedia. [13]

claims.claim: Facial exercise has measurable benefits for older adults
claims.believers: Instructors and programmes promote face exercise for wellbeing as well as looks.
claims.experts: A Japanese study of adults aged 65 to 87 assessed facial exercises for mental health, and another trial studied hand and face exercises in mild cognitive impairment. [3][4]

angle.goal: Facial muscle tone, cheeks and jawline
chain: Proponents expect firmer, bulkier facial muscles
Fuller cheeks, tighter-looking contours and smoother lines (claimed)
angle.text: People do face exercises to firm and fill the cheeks, define the chin and jaw, and soften expression lines without a procedure. In forum discussion it is a low-cost, no-equipment option often mentioned for people who are young or have limited budgets.
